title: map, filter and reduce
summary: Transform every item, keep some items, or combine them all into one value, without writing the loop yourself.

sections.heading: map: change every item
body: `map` runs a function on each item and gives you a new list of the results. Python usually writes this as a list comprehension.

sections.heading: filter: keep some items
body: `filter` keeps only the items where your function returns true.

python.code: print([n for n in [1, 2, 3, 4] if n % 2 == 0])

sections.heading: reduce: combine into one value
body: `reduce` carries a running value through the list, like a total. Always give it a starting value (here `0`).
For plain sums Python has `sum`, which is easier to read.

python.code:
from functools import reduce
print(reduce(lambda total, n: total + n, [1, 2, 3, 4], 0))
print(sum([1, 2, 3, 4]))

sections.heading: Chaining them
body: Each step returns a new list, so you can line them up: keep the paid orders, take their prices, add them up. Read it top to bottom like a recipe.

javascript.code:
const orders = [
  { item: 'tea', price: 3, paid: true },
  { item: 'cake', price: 5, paid: false },
  { item: 'pie', price: 4, paid: true },
]
const paidTotal = orders
  .filter((o) => o.paid)
  .map((o) => o.price)
  .reduce((sum, p) => sum + p, 0)
console.log(paidTotal)

python.code:
orders = [
    {'item': 'tea', 'price': 3, 'paid': True},
    {'item': 'cake', 'price': 5, 'paid': False},
    {'item': 'pie', 'price': 4, 'paid': True},
]
paid_total = sum(o['price'] for o in orders if o['paid'])
print(paid_total)

mistakes: Leaving out the starting value of `reduce`: it then fails on an empty list.
Using `map` just to loop when you do not need the new list. Use `for` (or `forEach`) for that.
Arrow functions with braces need `return`, or every result is `undefined`.
